tip: ‘cyn' plus a verb-noun means before doing something: ‘cyn dechrau' = before starting, with no word for who does it.
One passive is ‘cael ei' plus a soft-mutated verb: ‘paentio' becomes ‘ei baentio', so the house is being painted.
Feminine nouns usually soften after ‘y' (the): ‘cath' becomes ‘y gath', while masculine ‘bwrdd' stays as ‘y bwrdd'.
Welsh puts illnesses on you with ‘ar': ‘mae peswch arna i' is literally a cough is on me, not I have a cough.
The feminine ‘ei' (its/her) adds h to a verb starting with a vowel: ‘anfon' becomes ‘ei hanfon' here.
‘caiff' plus ‘ei' plus a soft-mutated verb is a passive: ‘caiff y gwaith ei wneud' = the work will be done.
‘ar ôl i' plus a person plus a softened verb means after someone does: ‘ar ôl i fi orffen' = after I finish.
With ‘ers', a present-tense verb means have been doing: ‘dyn ni'n byw yn y dref ers blwyddyn' = we have been living for a year.
‘pe bai' sets up an unreal if: ‘pe bai'r siop ar agor' = if the shop were open, matched by ‘byddwn i', I would.
‘mae angen' plus a verb-noun means something needs doing: ‘mae angen atgyweirio'r car' = the car needs repairing.
‘mae gen i' means I have, and the thing owned softens: ‘bocs' becomes ‘focs' in ‘mae gen i focs bwyd'.
The ending -wyd makes a past passive with no named doer: ‘agorwyd yr amgueddfa' = the museum was opened.
In a passive, ‘gan' marks who did it (by): ‘agorwyd yr amgueddfa gan y Frenhines' = opened by the Queen.
Two has a feminine form ‘dwy' (masculine ‘dau'), used with feminine nouns: ‘ddwy nofel' = two novels.
The relative ‘a' (that/which) softens the following verb: ‘darllenais' becomes ‘y llyfr a ddarllenais', the book that I read.
‘rhaid i' plus a person plus a softened verb means must: ‘rhaid i ni weithredu' = we must act (‘gweithredu' to ‘weithredu').
The feminine ‘ei' changes c to ch: ‘canslo' becomes ‘ei chanslo', so ‘y gêm' was cancelled.
The -wch ending makes a plural or polite command: ‘paratowch' means prepare (you).
Welsh forms a passive with ‘cael ei' plus a verb-noun: ‘cael ei thrwsio' means is being repaired.
‘gwnaed' is the irregular impersonal past of ‘gwneud' (do or make): ‘gwnaed y penderfyniad' means the decision was made.
The verb ‘ymweld' takes ‘â' for what is visited: ‘ymwelodd hi â'i mam-gu' means she visited her grandmother.
Dates use an ordinal with ‘o' for of: ‘y pedwerydd o Ebrill' means the fourth of April.
After the feminine ‘ei' (its), c, p and t take an added h: ‘cynnal' becomes ‘ei chynnal' here.
‘fe'i' is the particle ‘fe' plus the object pronoun ‘i' (him or her): ‘fe'i penodwyd' means he was appointed.
Feminine nouns usually soft-mutate after the article ‘yr' or ‘'r': ‘prifysgol' becomes ‘i'r brifysgol' here.
A verb-noun can act as a subject like an -ing noun: ‘mae teithio'n ehangu' means travelling broadens.
The -wyd ending is the impersonal past, a passive with no named doer: ‘sefydlwyd yr ysgol' means the school was founded.
To name the doer after an impersonal verb, add ‘gan' (by): ‘gan Aneirin' means by Aneirin.
Welsh has no plain verb to need. ‘mae angen' plus a verb-noun does it: ‘mae angen gweithredu' means action is needed.
‘mae' plus ‘yn' plus a verb-noun is the present tense: ‘mae'r myfyrwyr yn astudio' means the students study.
